titulo: A small business is not a small company: the DICA method
lead: A nine-person clinic is not a miniature big company. The owner decides alone, there's no IT, WhatsApp is the front door to everything, and a lot of the rules live in her head. That's why the diagnosis comes before any tool, and it's where the DICA method starts.
objetivo: describe the small business in 5 lines and place the diagnosis (D) within the DICA method before proposing any AI.

aprende.t: What changes in a business where the owner decides everything
The four letters of DICA and what comes out of each one
The 5-line sheet that opens every diagnosis
Where the DICA Program fits into Professional 2030

hero_alt: A small workshop owner and a consultant looking together at a notebook on the counter.

secoes.sub: Four steps, in this order. This course is the D. Click each letter.

nos.detalhe: Interview the owner, score the 5 areas, pull out of their head the rules nobody wrote down, and deliver a one-page map with a recommendation. What comes out of here: the report and the 30-day plan.
Choose the first assistant, write its playbook, and turn it on with approval in phases. It only starts once the diagnosis has said what to do and what not to do.
Teach the owner and one person on the team how to use it, fix it, and ask for adjustments. Without this, the assistant dies when the consultant leaves.
A short check-in every week, a few indicators, and an alert when something goes off track, until the assistant runs on its own.

secoes.volta: the follow-up brings the next area into a new diagnosis
secoes.legenda: Building got easy; trusting what was built did not. The D is where trust begins.

secoes.titulo: The portrait of the small business
secoes.sub: Four traits that change how you diagnose.

texto: There is no board and no purchasing department. The person who answers the interview is the one who approves, pays, and uses it.
That speeds up the decision, but everything depends on one person's schedule and mood.

exemplo.texto: The owner sees patients in the morning and handles administration in the afternoon. The conversation with you fits between the two.

texto: The system password, the WhatsApp account, and the spreadsheet stay with whoever set them up, sometimes a nephew.
Before you think about integrating, find out who has access to what.
Scheduling, questions, complaints, and payments all arrive on the same phone.
That's why the WhatsApp rules (lesson 7) belong in the diagnosis, not only in the build.

passos.titulo: The rules live in their head
texto: The owner knows how to do it but not how to describe it. Prices, exceptions, and "the way we do things here" were never written down.
Lessons 4 and 5 teach you how to draw this out without asking the owner to come up with rules alone.

secoes.sub: Fill it in before the interview with what you already know; the rest becomes questions. Replace what is between < > with your own.

blocos.conteudo:
# 5-line sheet — <business name> (<city>, <date>)

1. Who decides: <name and role; who else needs to agree>
2. Main channel: <how the customer arrives and talks: WhatsApp, phone, counter>
3. Who answers today: <person, hours, what happens outside hours>
4. What can't stop: <the activity that, if it stops for a day, costs money>
5. Where the information lives: <system, spreadsheet, notebook, someone's head>

Don't know yet: <what is missing and which interview question will answer it>

# 5-line sheet — Clínica Vila Serena (fictional)

1. Who decides: the owner, alone; the partner weighs in on spending
2. Main channel: the front desk WhatsApp (one phone)
3. Who answers today: the receptionist, 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.; at night, the owner on her own phone
4. What can't stop: the physical therapists' schedule
5. Where the information lives: schedule in the clinic's system; prices and insurance plans in the team's heads

Don't know yet: how many messages arrive per day (interview question 5)

abas.html:
• Each line has a concrete answer (a name, a channel, a place), not an adjective.
  • There is at least one "don't know yet" line, tied to an interview question.
  • No line mentions an AI tool.

• Writing the solution on the sheet ("needs a robot").
  • Leaving line 1 vague: "the company decides".
  • Making up what you don't know instead of marking "don't know yet".

secoes.sub: Four and a half minutes: the conversation, the one-page diagnosis, and a clinic example.
Clínica Vila Serena is fictional and stays with you throughout the course.

exercicios.texto: Copy the template and fill it in for Clínica Vila Serena (physical therapy and aesthetics, 9 people, an owner who sees patients and handles administration, front desk on WhatsApp). If you serve a real business, do theirs too, with permission.
exercicios.pronto: the 5 lines have concrete answers and at least one is marked "don't know yet", with the question that will answer it.

exercicios.titulo: E2 · The D separate from the sale
exercicios.texto: Write one sentence on what your diagnosis delivers and one sentence on what it does not deliver (price, building, promise of results).
exercicios.pronto: both sentences exist, and the second one names at least one thing that is left for after the diagnosis.

perguntas.p: In a small business, the person you interview in the diagnosis is usually:
opcoes: A purchasing committee with three departments.
The owner, who decides, pays, and uses it.
A representative from the system vendor.
perguntas.explica: With no board and no IT department, the owner is the one who decides and the one who uses it. The common mistake is preparing the conversation as if it were for a big company, with technical terms and several meetings.

perguntas.p: What comes out of step D of the DICA method?
opcoes: A one-page report with a recommendation and a 30-day plan.
The assistant already running on the company's WhatsApp, serving customers.
The signed contract with a fixed price.
perguntas.explica: D delivers the map and the recommendation. Building is I, teaching is C, and price belongs to Selling with AI.

perguntas.p: In the 5-line sheet, the "I don't know yet" line is for:
opcoes: Showing the owner that they forgot to share something.
Filling in later with a guess.
Justifying a higher price for the diagnosis.
Linking what's missing to a question in the interview.
perguntas.explica: What you don't know becomes a question. Making up the answer is the mistake that contaminates the rest of the diagnosis.

perguntas.p: Why do the WhatsApp rules come into the diagnosis right away?
opcoes: Because the diagnosis already chooses the tool.
Because almost everything in a small business goes through it, and the rule changes what you can recommend.
Because Meta requires a written diagnosis before it approves any business account on the platform.
Because WhatsApp is the only area that matters.
perguntas.explica: Scheduling, questions, and payments all come in through the same phone. Recommending something the platform's rules don't allow is a diagnosis mistake, not a building mistake.

itens.texto: An owner who decides alone, no IT department, WhatsApp at the center, and the rules in their head. The diagnosis starts from there.
Diagnose, Implement, Coach, Accompany. Nothing gets built before D says what to do and what not to do.
Who decides, channel, who answers, what can't stop, and where the information lives. What's missing becomes a question.
